prompt: What does the interface segregation principle say?

choices.text: Every interface must have exactly one method
choices.why: Size is not the measure; five methods every client calls is well segregated.

choices.text: No client should depend on methods it does not use
choices.why: Right. The question is who uses an interface, asked per kind of client.

choices.text: A class should implement at most one interface so its purpose stays clear
choices.why: The Library class plays three roles at once, and that is the point of role interfaces.

prompt: The OneTitle stand-in implemented search and Python refused to create it. How many abstract methods did the error message name?
In production the kiosk works fine with the fat Catalogue. Where does the cost of the fat interface show first?

choices.text: In slower searches, since six methods are loaded
choices.why: Unused methods cost nothing at run time; the cost is in what has to be written and changed.

choices.text: In a test double for the kiosk
choices.why: Right. And every later change to those methods means editing that double too.

choices.text: In the kiosk's output
choices.why: The output is correct; nothing the kiosk prints depends on the other methods.

choices.text: In the database, which needs one table per interface method
choices.why: No database is involved; interfaces say nothing about storage.

prompt: How does the lesson fix ReferenceBook without any class refusing anything?

choices.text: Lending becomes a separate Lendable protocol that only some items satisfy
choices.why: Right. The reference book stops claiming a capability it does not have.

choices.text: ReferenceBook.lend returns None instead of raising
choices.why: That weakens the postcondition; it is lesson 3's Laptop problem in another form.

choices.text: check_out skips reference books with an isinstance test
choices.why: That puts the fix in every caller, the symptom lesson 3 warned about.

prompt: Match each symptom of a fat interface to where the course showed it.

pairs.left: a test double stubs methods the test never touches
a change to one method rebuilds unrelated clients

prompt: A team has a class with fifteen methods and needs an interface for testing. They lift all fifteen into it. What does the section predict?

choices.text: Nothing bad: the interface matches the class exactly, so it is always correct
choices.why: Matching the class is the problem: it describes the implementer, not what any client needs.

choices.text: Every client inherits the class's whole surface
choices.why: Right. The interface was shaped by the implementer; asking each client what it calls gives the better names.

choices.text: Python will refuse an interface with more than ten methods
choices.why: Python sets no such limit; the cost is in dependencies, not in a rule of the language.

choices.text: The class will have to be split into fifteen classes
choices.why: Segregating interfaces splits declarations; the class can stay whole.

prompt: In roles.py, Library plays three roles but names none of the protocols. Why does that work?

choices.text: Because Protocol classes register every class automatically
choices.why: Nothing is registered; a protocol describes a shape and checks nothing at run time.

choices.text: Because Library inherits from all three through object
choices.why: object is the parent of every class and knows nothing of these protocols.

choices.text: Python matches by shape: having the methods is enough
choices.why: Right. Java is the exception, where the class must say implements for each role.

prompt: The desk starts taking books back as well as lending them. Where does give_back go?

choices.text: Into Lending, since the same client calls both and they change together
choices.why: Right. A role is the set of methods one kind of client uses, whatever its size.

choices.text: Into a new GivingBack protocol, since a role must have one method
choices.why: Two names for one client's needs buy nothing; one method per role is not the rule.

choices.text: Into Searching, the kiosk's role
choices.why: The kiosk never takes books back; putting it there would fatten the kiosk's interface.

choices.text: Nowhere: give_back stays outside every protocol
choices.why: Then the desk could not ask for it through its role.

prompt: In Go, small interfaces such as io.Reader are usually declared in the package of the ___ that uses them, not beside the type that implements them.
What, according to the section, decides whether dependencies have been inverted?

choices.text: Whether objects are passed in rather than built inside
choices.why: That is dependency injection; you can inject a concrete mail class and invert nothing.

choices.text: Who owns the abstraction, and which way the imports point
choices.why: Right. The rules own the port, and the detail imports it.

choices.text: Whether there is an interface anywhere between the two classes
choices.why: An interface beside the mail code, mirroring its methods, still leaves the rules depending on the mail package.

prompt: A team adds IMailer with send_mail(address, subject, body), in the mail package, and has the rules use it. Why is the inversion still missing?

choices.text: The name starts with I, which Python does not allow for classes
choices.why: Python forbids no names; the problem is whose words the abstraction uses and where it lives.

choices.text: It has three parameters, and a port must have exactly one
choices.why: The parameter count is not the issue; notify itself has two.

choices.text: It is the detail's vocabulary, in the detail's package
choices.why: Right. Switching to SMS would still mean changing it; a Notifier in the rules' module would not.

prompt: Dependency inversion: high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on ___ .
The grep over the imports showed adapters.py importing from notices.py. What does that line prove?

choices.text: That the adapters cannot run without a mail server
choices.why: They print; the line is about which code knows which.

choices.text: The detail depends on the policy
choices.why: Right. That is the inversion, read off the file rather than a diagram.

choices.text: That notices.py imports the adapters indirectly through main.py
choices.why: notices.py imports only standard modules; main.py imports both, which is its job.

choices.text: That Python requires a Protocol to be imported before it is used
choices.why: The adapters would fit by shape without the import; naming it makes the direction visible.

prompt: OverdueNotices runs on 1 April 2026. A loan was lent on 9 March 2026. How many cents does its notice say?
hint: It is due 14 days after lending.

prompt: Every notice is to go by SMS from now on. Which files change? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: main.py
choices.why: Yes. Deciding which adapter the rules get is the wiring's job.

choices.text: notices.py
choices.why: No. The rules name only Notifier and never learn which one they were given.

choices.text: test_notices.py
choices.why: No. The test uses its own Recording double and imports no adapter.

choices.text: adapters.py
choices.why: No. SmsNotifier is already there.

prompt: Match each piece of the notices program to its place in ports and adapters.
What is the one rule the section says the architecture comes down to?

choices.text: The project has folders called domain, ports and adapters
choices.why: The folders are optional; a project can have them and break the rule.

choices.text: Every class is drawn inside a hexagon
choices.why: The hexagon only leaves room to draw several ports; it means nothing else.

choices.text: Nothing in the middle imports anything at the edge
choices.why: Right. The same rule the grep checked in the previous section.

prompt: Why does the section call every abstraction in overdone.py speculative?

choices.text: Because abstract classes are slower than functions
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; both programs print 250 instantly.

choices.text: Because each one has exactly one implementation
choices.why: Right. An abstraction with one implementation separates nothing from anything.

choices.text: Because Python has no interfaces, so ABCs in Python are always a mistake
choices.why: Lesson 2 used an ABC well for Notice; the problem is a seam nobody uses.

prompt: wc -l counted the two versions of the fine. How many more lines did overdone.py have than plain.py?
Put the life of the fine rule in the order the section describes, from today to later.
items: A plain function with one constant
Students get grace days: PerDay and GraceDays parts
The rules need testing without mail: a Notifier port
Each seam named after the change that brought it
trap: The ports come after the change that needs them, never before; starting with the interfaces is overdone.py.

prompt: A ReminderService needs only to look up a member's phone. It is given the whole MemberRepository, with eleven methods. Which principle does that strain, and what is the fix?

choices.text: Interface segregation: a small PhoneLookup role, declared by the reminders
choices.why: Right. The repository can still be the object passed in; the reminders just ask for less.

choices.text: Liskov substitution: the repository cannot be replaced
choices.why: No child breaks a parent's promise here; the issue is how much the client depends on.

choices.text: Single responsibility: split MemberRepository into eleven classes
choices.why: Splitting by method is splitting by size; the client's declaration is what should shrink.

prompt: A colleague says: "We use dependency injection everywhere, so our code follows dependency inversion." The rules receive an SmtpMailer through their constructor. Is the colleague right?

choices.text: Yes: passing the object in is what inversion means
choices.why: Passing in is injection; what the rules are typed against still belongs to the mail code.

choices.text: No: the rules still depend on a mail class; they need a port of their own
choices.why: Right. Injection is a technique; inversion is about who owns the abstraction and which way imports point.

choices.text: Yes, as long as SmtpMailer has an interface somewhere
choices.why: An interface owned by the mail package, in its vocabulary, inverts nothing.

choices.text: No: inversion is impossible in Python, which has no interfaces
choices.why: notices.py did it with a Protocol; every language in the course can.

prompt: A new project starts with IBookRepository, BookRepositoryImpl and a BookRepositoryFactory, though one storage is planned and no test uses a double. What does this lesson advise?

choices.text: Keep them: SOLID requires an interface for every repository
choices.why: No principle says that; each is conditional on a change.

choices.text: Add a second implementation so the interface is justified
choices.why: That builds more code to excuse the first speculation.

choices.text: Start plain, and add the port when a real change asks for it
choices.why: Right. A seam arrives with the change that justifies it, and takes its name from that change.
